statement: Care about your craft: only develop software if you intend to do it well — caring about quality is a precondition, not an optional extra.
Think continuously and critically about your work, appraising every decision as you make it rather than running on auto-pilot.
There is no single best tool, language, or operating system; choose the option most appropriate to the specific circumstances rather than committing permanently to one technology.
Maintain a broad grounding in computer-science fundamentals plus a wide base of practical experience so you can select good solutions for particular situations.
Invest small amounts of effort every day to refine existing skills and add new ones (continuous improvement / kaizen) rather than relying on occasional large pushes.
Core pragmatic techniques are universal: modularity, for example, applies to code, designs, documentation, and team organization, not just to source code.
Take responsibility for your career, your projects, and your day-to-day work, and do not be afraid to admit ignorance or error.
Responsibility is actively agreed to: when you accept responsibility for an outcome, expect to be held accountable for it.
You have the right to decline responsibility for an impossible situation or one whose risks are too great, deciding by your own ethics and judgment.
condition: when the situation is impossible or the uncontrollable risks are too great

statement: When you make a mistake or error in judgment, admit it honestly and provide options to salvage the situation instead of excuses or blame.
Anticipate risks beyond your control and prepare a contingency plan, such as keeping backups or planning for a vendor failing to deliver.
Before delivering bad news, rehearse the conversation and arrive with concrete options such as refactoring, prototyping, better testing, automation, or a request for help.
Do not live with broken windows: fix bad designs, wrong decisions, and poor code as soon as they are discovered.
If there is not enough time to fix a flaw properly, board it up by commenting out the offending code, showing a Not Implemented message, or substituting dummy data to prevent further damage.
condition: when there is insufficient time to fix the flaw properly right now

statement: Neglect accelerates software rot faster than any other single factor, and the most important contributor to rot is the project's culture and psychology.
A single visible flaw left unrepaired signals abandonment and triggers further decay (the broken-window effect), so even one bad piece of code can start a project's decline.
Act as a catalyst for change: when you cannot get approval for a whole system, build something reasonable and demonstrable first, then let others rally to extend it.
Keep the big picture in view and constantly review what is happening around you, not just your own task, because most project disasters and overruns accumulate gradually.
Make quality a requirements issue: specify the intended scope and quality level of the system as part of its requirements.
Involve users in the quality trade-off and let them help decide when software is good enough, where good enough means adequate for users and maintainers, not sloppy.
Delivering good software early is often preferable to perfect software later, because early user feedback leads to a better eventual solution.
exception: safety-critical or widely disseminated software (e.g. pacemakers, avionics, broadly used libraries) where requirements are more stringent

statement: Know when to stop: do not spoil a good program with over-embellishment and over-refinement.
Treat your knowledge and experience as an expiring asset (a knowledge portfolio) that loses value over time and must be actively managed like a financial portfolio.
Invest in your knowledge portfolio regularly, even in small amounts, because the habit of investing matters more than the size of each investment.
Diversify your knowledge across many technologies and do not put all your technical eggs in one basket, balancing low-risk standards against risky high-reward emerging technologies.
Learn emerging technologies early to capture outsized payoff, and review and rebalance your skill set periodically as the industry shifts.
Set concrete learning goals such as learning at least one new language each year and reading a technical book each quarter, then monthly.

Broaden beyond your current stack by reading nontechnical books, taking classes, joining user groups, experimenting with different environments, and staying current via journals and online communities.
Learning a technology expands your thinking even if you never ship it, so cross-pollinate ideas from what you learn into your current project.
When you do not know an answer, treat finding it as a personal challenge by asking a guru, searching, or using the library, and build your professional network in the process.
Critically analyze what you read and hear so your knowledge stays accurate and unswayed by vendor or media hype, and beware zealots who claim their approach is the only answer.
Effective communication determines how influential you are, so treat communicating ideas as a core professional skill rather than an afterthought.
Plan what you want to say by writing an outline and refining it until it conveys your point, applying this to documents, meetings, and important calls alike.
Know your audience: understand their needs, interests, and capabilities, and tailor the same message to each group's priorities.
Choose your moment and style: make the message timely given the audience's current priorities, match the delivery format to them, and ask if unsure.
Presentation matters: do not undermine good content with poor-looking documents; use style sheets, page headers and footers, and spell-checking.
Make communication two-way: involve your audience with early drafts, listen by asking questions, and always get back to people who contact you.

Treat email as permanent and give it the same care as any written memo: proofread, keep the format simple, prefer plain text, minimize and attribute quoting, never flame, and check the recipient list.
Maintenance is not a discrete post-release phase; programmers are continuously in maintenance mode because understanding and requirements change throughout development.
Follow DRY: every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system.
Duplicated knowledge guarantees eventual inconsistency: if the same thing lives in two or more places, you will eventually forget to update one and create a contradiction.
Duplication arises in four forms (imposed, inadvertent, impatient, and interdeveloper), each requiring a different countermeasure.

When the environment forces multiple representations of the same information, generate the duplicates from one source with an active code generator that runs every build rather than a one-time conversion.
condition: when duplication is imposed by the environment, language, or multiple target platforms

statement: Keep low-level knowledge in the code and reserve comments for high-level explanation, because restating in comments what the code already expresses leads to drift, and untrustworthy comments are worse than none.
Generate tests programmatically from the specification so they stay in sync automatically when the specification changes.
Eliminate inadvertent duplication by normalizing data to the underlying business model and replacing derivable or mutually dependent fields with calculated fields.
Access object attributes only through accessor functions where possible, so behavior such as caching can be added later without changing callers (Uniform Access).
You may deliberately break DRY for performance, such as caching a computed value, but localize the violation so it is not exposed outside the owning module.
condition: when caching or another performance need justifies it

statement: Resist impatient copy-paste duplication under deadline pressure, because shortcuts taken now cause longer delays later.

Prevent interdeveloper duplication with clear design, a strong technical lead, divided responsibilities, frequent developer communication, a project librarian, a shared utility location, and routine reading of each other's code.
Make it easy to reuse: build an environment where finding and reusing existing code is easier than rewriting it, because if reuse is not easy people will not do it and will duplicate instead.
Two components are orthogonal when changes in one do not affect the other; design for this independence, for example keeping database code orthogonal to the user interface.
Nonorthogonal systems are inherently harder to change and control, because when components are highly interdependent there is no such thing as a local fix.
Eliminate effects between unrelated things: design self-contained components that are independent and each have a single, well-defined purpose (cohesion).
Orthogonal (decoupled) systems deliver two major benefits: increased productivity and reduced risk.
In orthogonal systems changes stay localized, cutting development and testing time, because small self-contained components are easier to build, test, and reuse than one large block.
Combining orthogonal components yields M x N distinct capabilities (more functionality per unit of effort), whereas nonorthogonal components overlap and deliver less.
Orthogonality reduces risk: defects stay isolated, the system is less fragile, it is easier to test, and you are less tightly bound to any single vendor, product, or platform.
Organize teams orthogonally into groups with well-defined responsibilities and minimal overlap, and gauge orthogonality by how many people must be involved in discussing each requested change.
Use layering to build orthogonal systems: each layer depends only on abstractions of the layers below, so implementations can change without affecting other code and runaway dependencies are reduced.
Apply an orthogonality test to a design: if one function's requirements change dramatically, ideally only one module should need to change.
Do not rely on properties of things you cannot control, such as using a telephone number as a customer identifier.

Preserve orthogonality when introducing third-party toolkits and libraries by isolating them behind well-defined abstract interfaces; a transparent integration is orthogonal, one that forces special access patterns is not.
Write shy code: modules that hide unnecessary detail and do not depend on other modules' implementations (Law of Demeter); to change an object's state, ask the object to do it.

Avoid global data, because each reference couples your code to every other component sharing it and breaks under change such as adding multithreading; pass required context explicitly and be wary of Singletons used as globals.
Treat duplicate or near-identical functions as a symptom of a structural problem and refactor them, for example via the Strategy pattern, rather than copying.
Build a unit test into every module and run all unit tests automatically as part of the build, because an orthogonal system pushes more testing down to the easier module level.
Use the difficulty of building a module's unit test as an orthogonality probe: if compiling or linking the test drags in much of the rest of the system, that module is poorly decoupled.
There are no final decisions: critical decisions are not easily reversible, so do not assume any decision is cast in stone and design to keep options open.
If you rely heavily on some fact, you can almost guarantee it will change.
Abstract third-party products behind well-defined interfaces (for example, treating a database as a persistence service) so you can switch vendors or technologies later.
Treat the deployment model (standalone, client-server, or n-tier) as a configuration choice; if switching it would take more than a few days, you have not designed for reversibility.
Maintain flexibility in architecture, deployment, and vendor integration (not just in code) using insulation so replacing one component does not ripple through the rest.
Whenever you inject cross-cutting requirements automatically via metadata, aspects, or scripts, make the mechanism reversible so what is added automatically can be removed automatically.
Use tracer bullets: build a thin but complete end-to-end skeleton of the system that works quickly, visibly, and repeatably, then incrementally flesh it out.
Tracer code is not a throwaway prototype: it is production-quality with error checking, structure, documentation, and self-checking, but it is not yet fully functional.

Prefer tracer-bullet incremental development because it lets users see working software early, gives developers a structure to build in, provides a daily integration platform instead of big-bang integration, always yields something to demo, and gives a truer feel for progress.
Tracer code's small size gives it low inertia, so you can gather feedback and produce a more accurate version faster and at less cost than heavier methods.
Tracer bullets reveal what you are actually hitting, which may not be the target, so expect early misses and adjust aim; use the technique when you are not certain where you are going.
condition: when you are not 100 percent certain where the system is going

statement: Tracer code differs from a prototype: a prototype explores specific aspects and is then thrown away and recoded, whereas tracer code is lean but complete and becomes part of the final system's skeleton.
Build prototypes to analyze and expose risk and to allow correction at greatly reduced cost, targeting each prototype at specific aspects of the system.
Prototypes need not be code: use Post-it notes, whiteboard sketches, or non-functional mock-ups to prototype workflow, application logic, and user interfaces.
A prototype answers only a few questions, so it may ignore correctness, completeness, robustness, and style when those details are unimportant for the question being explored.

Prototype anything that carries risk: anything new, unproven, experimental, critical, or that you are uncomfortable with, such as architecture, new functionality, external data, third-party tools, performance, or UI design.
Prototype to learn: the value of a prototype lies in the lessons learned, not in the code produced.

Implement prototypes in a very high-level or scripting language such as Perl, Python, or Tcl to defer details and produce functional code quickly, and use such languages as glue to combine low-level pieces.
exception: when measuring absolute rather than relative performance, where a language close to the target's performance is required

statement: You can prototype architecture without writing code using a whiteboard, Post-its, or index cards, checking whether component responsibilities and collaborations are well defined, coupling is minimized, duplication sources exist, interfaces are acceptable, and every module has a timely access path to the data it needs.
Before code-based prototyping, ensure everyone understands the code is disposable, incomplete, and cannot be completed, so sponsors or management do not insist on deploying it.
If there is a strong risk that prototype code will be misinterpreted as deployable, use the tracer-bullet approach instead to end up with a solid framework.
condition: when the purpose of prototype code may be misinterpreted in your environment or culture

statement: Used properly, a prototype saves significant time, money, and pain by identifying and correcting problem spots early, when fixing mistakes is cheap and easy.
The programming language you use shapes how you think about a problem, and the vocabulary of the problem domain can itself suggest a programming solution.
Write code using the vocabulary of the application domain, supported by a project glossary.
Program close to the problem domain: consider a mini-language that lets you work at the domain's level of abstraction so you can focus on domain problems and ignore petty implementation details.
A domain mini-language can begin as a non-executable specification that captures user requirements and later be implemented so the specification becomes executable code.
Programming in the problem domain lets you perform domain-specific validation and report errors in the user's own vocabulary rather than generic compiler messages.
Provide mini-languages or mini-environments for each class of user (end users, operations, configuration and test managers, support, and future developers), since each has its own problem domain.

Implement a simple mini-language as a line-oriented, easily parsed format using switch statements or regular expressions; for a more complex one, specify the grammar first in BNF and feed it to a parser generator such as yacc, bison, or javaCC.
Distinguish data languages, which compile to a data structure such as configuration, from imperative languages, which are executed and contain control constructs.

A mini-language need not be executed by the application directly; it can generate artifacts and metadata such as SQL, C, web pages, and XML from one schema specification that the program then consumes.
Embedding a high-level imperative language in your application lets you change behavior by editing scripts without recompiling, which simplifies maintenance in a dynamic domain.

When choosing a mini-language grammar, prefer the more complex but readable real-language form up front, because most applications outlive their expected lifetimes and the extra effort is repaid in reduced support and maintenance costs.
Estimate to avoid surprises: developing an intuitive feel for the magnitudes of things lets you judge feasibility quickly.

Match an estimate's accuracy to its context, and choose the units of your answer to convey the accuracy you intend, for example quoting about six months rather than 130 days when you do not mean day-level precision.
A reliable estimating shortcut is to ask someone who has already done something similar before building a model from scratch.
Begin any estimate by understanding what is being asked and grasping the scope of the domain, since the scope you choose becomes part of your answer.
Build a rough mental model of the system to estimate, because the modeling process itself surfaces underlying patterns and can let you reframe the original question.
Decompose the estimation model into components, identify each component's parameters, and work out how the parameters combine into the result.

Concentrate estimating accuracy on the parameters with the most impact (those multiplied or divided matter more than those added), and have a justifiable way to calculate the critical ones, for example by measuring an existing system.
Beware estimates built on sub-estimates, because that is where the largest errors accumulate.
When a calculated estimate seems strange but the arithmetic is correct, treat it as a signal that your understanding or model is probably wrong rather than as noise.
Record your estimates and compare them to actuals, and when one is wrong, find out why so the next estimate improves.

Iterate the schedule with the code: for non-trivial projects, determine the timetable by gaining experience through incremental development (check requirements, analyze risk, design and implement and integrate, validate with users), refining the iteration plan after each increment.
When put on the spot for an estimate, answer that you will get back to them and work through the estimation steps, because off-the-cuff estimates come back to haunt you.
Tools amplify your talent, so the better your tools and the better you know them the more productive you are; start with a basic generally applicable set and let genuine need drive new acquisitions.
Do not confine yourself to a single power tool such as one IDE; keep a sharp command-line tool set so you can work beyond any IDE's built-in limits.
Keep knowledge in plain text, because human-readable plain text is the best format for storing knowledge persistently and lets you manipulate it with virtually every available tool.
Plain text is self-describing, keeping data together with the context needed to understand it, whereas binary formats divorce data from its meaning.
Plain text's drawbacks are larger storage and higher processing cost; where those are unacceptable, store metadata about the raw data in plain text instead.
condition: when the storage or processing cost of full plain text is unacceptable, e.g. satellite telemetry or a relational database's internal format

statement: Binary data is more obscure but no more secure than plain text; to protect sensitive values, encrypt them or guard configuration with a secure hash checksum rather than relying on a binary format.

Prefer human-readable, self-describing data because it outlives the applications that created it and can be parsed with only partial knowledge of its format, and use meaningful names and tags (for example SSNO rather than FIELD10).
The Unix philosophy of small, sharp tools that each do one thing well is enabled by a common line-oriented plain-text format.
Treat the command shell as your workbench: combine tools with pipes, automate repetitive tasks, and build custom macro commands beyond what any single tool was designed to do.
GUIs can be faster for some simple operations but are limited to what their designers intended, so use the command line for ad hoc operations and automation that GUIs cannot support.
Use the power of command shells: gaining familiarity with the shell raises productivity, and shell commands combine into scripts that automate frequent tasks.
Use a single editor well: know one editor thoroughly and use it for all editing tasks (code, documentation, memos, administration) so text manipulation becomes reflexive.
Choose an editor that is available on every platform you work on.
Insist your editor be configurable, extensible to new languages and formats, and programmable via macros or a scripting language.
Prefer keystroke-based editing over mouse and menu commands, because keeping your hands on the keyboard and moving by words, lines, blocks, or functions is far more efficient.

Exploit editor features such as syntax highlighting (which surfaces mistyped keywords before you compile), auto-completion, auto-indentation for consistent project style, boilerplate templates, and in-editor compile-and-navigate-to-error.
Always use source code control, for everything including documentation, configuration, and build scripts and even throwaway prototypes, and even when you are a one-person team on a one-week project.
Source code control is a project-wide time machine: with it you can always return to a previous version and recover from mistakes made long ago.

Source code control also lets you track who changed what and when, identify and regenerate any release, manage release branches separately from trunk development, and coordinate concurrent multi-user edits via managed merging.
Putting an entire project under source code control enables automatic, repeatable builds that pull the latest source, run unattended with regression tests, and need no manual copy steps.
If your team will not adopt source code control, set up your own private repository for your work anyway.
Treat debugging as problem solving rather than an emotional or blame exercise, since no one writes perfect software and debugging will consume a major part of your time.
Fix the problem, not the blame: whether a bug is your fault or someone else's, it is still your problem to solve.
Don't panic when debugging: step back and reason about what could cause the symptoms, and never dismiss a reported bug as impossible, because it clearly can and did happen.
Avoid debugging myopia: fix the root cause, which may be several steps removed from the symptom, rather than patching the symptom you happen to see.
Before debugging, ensure the code compiles cleanly with no warnings, and set compiler warning levels as high as possible so the compiler finds problems for you.
Be accurate in your observations and do not be misled by coincidences; when a bug report is second-hand, watch or interview the user who reported it to gather enough detail.
Test both boundary conditions and realistic end-user usage patterns systematically, because artificial or narrow tests fail to exercise enough of the application to expose bugs.
Make a bug reproducible, ideally with a single command, before trying to fix it, because isolating the circumstances both confirms a fix and often reveals it.
Visualize the data a program operates on, from simple variable-equals-value output to richer debugger or plotting views, to discern what the program is doing.

Use tracing statements in a consistent, parseable format to observe program and data state over time, especially in concurrent, real-time, and event-based systems where state-snapshot debuggers fall short.
When a variable looks corrupted, examine the surrounding memory for clues before deeper debugging.
Use rubber ducking: explain the problem step by step to another person or even an object, because verbalizing the assumptions you take for granted often makes the cause leap out.

Assume a bug is in your own application code rather than the OS, compiler, or a third-party library, and eliminate your code first even when a third party is genuinely at fault (if you see hoof prints, think horses, not zebras).

If something broke right after you changed only one thing, that change is most likely responsible however farfetched it seems, and changes outside your control such as new OS, compiler, or database versions can also break previously correct code.
When you upgrade third-party software such as the OS, compiler, or database, retest the system under the new conditions and weigh the timing, since you may want to wait until after your next release.
When you have no obvious place to start, localize a bug with a binary search through the code.

Don't assume it, prove it: a surprising failure means one of your assumptions is wrong, so prove the suspect code actually works in this context, with this data and these boundary conditions, instead of trusting code you think you know works.

After fixing a surprising bug, determine why it escaped earlier: amend tests to catch it, add earlier parameter checking, find and fix the same defect elsewhere, make the next fix easier, and discuss wrong-assumption bugs with the whole team.
Learn a text-manipulation language such as awk, sed, Python, Tcl, or Perl, because it lets you hack utilities and prototype ideas five to ten times faster than conventional languages.
Write code that writes code: a code generator, once built, is reused throughout a project at virtually no cost, cutting repetitive typing and mistakes.

Distinguish passive code generators, which run once and whose output becomes freestanding source, from active code generators, which run whenever output is needed and whose output is disposable and regenerated.
Passive code generators need not be totally accurate; choose how much effort to invest in the generator versus fixing its output by hand.

Use active code generators to honor DRY by generating every needed form from one representation, and to meld disparate environments such as a database schema and its access code, so a source change updates derived code automatically and errors surface at compile time.
condition: only when the code generation is made part of the build process

statement: Keep a code generator's input format simple so the generator itself stays simple.
Code generators need not produce program source; they can generate HTML, XML, plain text, or any artifact that feeds another part of the project.
Accept that you cannot write perfect software as an axiom, so you stop wasting energy chasing an impossible dream and instead plan for failure.
Code defensively: validate all information you are given, use assertions to detect bad data, check consistency, and constrain database columns, and do not even trust your own code.
Use Design by Contract: document and verify each software module's rights and responsibilities, where a correct program does no more and no less than it claims to do.

Specify each routine's preconditions (what must be true to call it, which the caller is responsible for satisfying), postconditions (what it guarantees on completion, implying it terminates), and class invariants (conditions always true from a caller's perspective).

Read the contract as: if the caller meets every precondition, the routine guarantees all postconditions and invariants on completion, and any failure to meet the contract is a bug that should never happen.
Do not use preconditions to perform user-input validation, because a precondition violation is a bug rather than an expected runtime condition.
Design with contracts by writing lazy code: be strict in what you accept before you begin and promise as little as possible in return.

Follow the Liskov Substitution Principle: a subclass must be usable through its base-class interface without the caller knowing the difference, accepting at least as much input and guaranteeing at least as much as its parent, though it may accept wider input or promise more.

Specify a contract once in the base class so it applies to every subclass automatically, because without contracts the compiler can only check method signatures, not that the methods preserve their meaning.

The greatest benefit of Design by Contract is forcing requirements and guarantees to the forefront at design time (the input domain, boundary conditions, and what the routine does and does not promise), which is the antidote to programming by coincidence.
Even in a language without DBC support, write the contract as comments, since DBC is fundamentally a design technique that still gives a place to start when trouble strikes.

Recognize that assertions only partially emulate Design by Contract: they do not propagate down an inheritance hierarchy, have no built-in concept of old entry values, and do not check the runtime system or libraries.

Prefer languages with built-in DBC such as Eiffel or Sather for automatic precondition and postcondition checking across the whole code base, and otherwise use preprocessors such as Nana for C and C++ or iContract for Java.
When a postcondition references a passed-in parameter, prevent the routine from modifying that parameter, for example with Java's final, so the contract cannot be circumvented.
Express a function's valid domain in its precondition, which shifts the burden of correctness to the caller where it belongs and lets the routine assume valid input.
Crashing early at the site of a problem is far easier to diagnose than returning a special value like NaN that only explodes much later.
Give every case or switch statement a default clause so you find out when the impossible value occurs.

Use a loop invariant (a generalized statement of the loop's goal that holds before the loop and after every iteration) to get boundary conditions right and as a design and documentation aid, optionally coded as an assertion.
Capture inviolate requirements as semantic invariants central to the meaning of the system, document them clearly and unambiguously, and distinguish them from mere policies that may change.
Design a piece of software's contract whenever you design the software, because you cannot automate contracts such as for autonomous agents if you cannot specify them by hand.
Treat every error as information and reject the it-cannot-happen mentality: assume that if an error occurs, something very bad has happened.
Crash early: detect problems as soon as possible and terminate, because a dead program does far less damage than a crippled one writing corrupted data or driving a device into a bad state.

When something supposedly impossible happens, treat the program as no longer viable and terminate it as soon as possible, since everything it does afterward is suspect; use exceptions to clean up resources if needed.
If you think something can never happen, add an assertion to ensure it will not.
Do not use assertions in place of real error handling, because assertions check for things that should never happen, not for expected runtime conditions.
Ensure the condition evaluated in an assertion has no side effects, or you create a Heisenbug where the check itself changes behavior.

Leave assertions turned on in production, because testing never exercises more than a tiny fraction of real permutations and production faces hazards testing does not; turn off only the specific assertions with a real performance cost.
Use exceptions to move error handling to a single place and keep the normal flow of control clear, instead of deeply nested return-code checks.
Use exceptions only for exceptional problems, reserving them for unexpected events; test this by asking whether the code would still run correctly if every exception handler were removed.

Decide whether a condition like a missing file warrants an exception by whether the resource should have been there: if it should exist, raise an exception; if its existence is genuinely unknown, return an error instead.
condition: depends on whether the resource was expected to exist

statement: Avoid using exceptions in normal processing, because they act as a cascading goto that produces spaghetti-like code and breaks encapsulation by coupling routines to their callers.
Consider error handlers as an alternative or complement to exceptions, especially in languages without exceptions or to avoid tedious per-call handling such as RMI's RemoteException.
Finish what you start: the routine or object that allocates a resource should be responsible for deallocating it.

Do not share resource handles through global variables across separate allocate and deallocate routines, because the coupling leaks resources under later maintenance; keep the open and close in the same scope so every open has a matching close.
When nesting allocations, deallocate resources in the reverse order of allocation to avoid orphaning references.
Always allocate the same set of resources in the same order everywhere in the code, to reduce the possibility of deadlock.

Encapsulate a resource in a class so its destructor or garbage collector deallocates it when the object goes out of scope, which is especially valuable where exceptions can interfere with manual deallocation.
Recognize that exceptions complicate deallocation: freeing the same resource in both the normal exit path and the catch handler violates DRY and invites maintenance bugs.

Free resources on every exit path: in C++ rely on automatic destruction of stack-local objects or wrap a resource in a class or auto_ptr, and in Java use a finally clause, which runs regardless of how the try block exits.

When the simple allocate-and-deallocate pattern does not fit, as with long-lived dynamic data structures, establish a semantic invariant that decides who is responsible for freeing aggregate data and implement that decision consistently.
When tracking resources by hand gets tricky, implement a reference-counting scheme to get limited automatic garbage collection.

Build code that actively checks resources are freed, using wrappers that track allocations and deallocations checked at a natural point such as the top of a server's main loop, and use leak-detection tools.

Write shy code in both directions: do not reveal yourself to other modules and do not interact with too many of them, organizing code into cells with limited interaction so a compromised module can be replaced.
Ask an object to perform a service on your behalf rather than fetching a third-party object to manipulate yourself, and do not traverse a chain of objects to reach a distant method.

Traversing object relationships directly causes a combinatorial explosion of dependencies, with symptoms such as a unit-test link command longer than the test, simple changes rippling through unrelated modules, and developers afraid to change code.
Minimize coupling between modules by applying the Law of Demeter, which forbids reaching through one object to call a third object's methods.
Empirically, classes with larger response sets are more error-prone, and because the Law of Demeter shrinks a class's response set, code following it tends to have fewer errors.

The Law of Demeter costs many forwarding wrapper methods with runtime and space overhead, so balance it against performance and deliberately reverse it to tightly couple modules only when that coupling is well known and acceptable.
exception: when a deliberate, well-known performance trade-off justifies tighter coupling

statement: Make logical and physical design proceed in tandem, because cyclic dependencies among files, directories, and libraries are extremely hard to undo and produce days-long build cycles.
Stay flexible by writing less code, since every code change risks introducing new bugs and moving details out of the code lets them change more safely.

Configure, don't integrate: implement deeply ingrained choices such as algorithms, database products, middleware, and UI style as configuration options driven by metadata rather than wiring them into the code.
Put abstractions in code and details in metadata: program for the general case and keep the specifics outside the compiled code base.

Driving an application from metadata forces a more decoupled, robust, abstract design, lets you customize and even work around production bugs without recompiling, expresses behavior closer to the problem domain, and lets one engine serve several projects via different metadata.

Maintain business policy and rules in a very flexible format such as configurable definitions, an embedded rule-based or expert system, or a mini-language, because they change more often than any other aspect of a project.
Represent configuration metadata in plain text.

Prefer programs that can reload their configuration while running over those that read it only at startup, weighing the extra complexity against use, since a long-running server benefits while a quickly restarting client GUI may not.
condition: justified mainly for long-running server processes

statement: Treat time, both concurrency and ordering, as a design element, because linear do-this-then-that thinking creates temporal coupling that is inflexible and unrealistic.
Decouple time and order dependencies and allow for concurrency to gain flexibility across workflow, architecture, design, and deployment.
Analyze workflow, for example with a UML activity diagram, to find what can happen in parallel versus what needs strict ordering, and maximize concurrency.
Designing components as independent, concurrently running entities (temporal decoupling) can make a system easier to write, not harder.

Design concurrent services that communicate via asynchronous work queues, where a process issues a request and immediately returns to its other work instead of blocking one service while another runs.

Use a hungry-consumer model for load balancing: replace a central scheduler with independent consumer tasks pulling from a shared work queue, so a bogged-down task does not block the others and each proceeds at its own pace.
Design using services: independent, concurrent objects behind well-defined, consistent interfaces.
Treat concurrency's constraints as beneficial, because they force you to think through time-based dependencies, decouple your code, and fight programming by coincidence.
Protect every global or static variable from concurrent access, and use the need for protection as a prompt to question why the global exists at all.

Ensure an object is in a valid state whenever it could possibly be called, since a concurrent system may call it at awkward times; class invariants help avoid the separate-constructor-then-initialize trap.

Designing for concurrency leads to cleaner interfaces: avoid hidden state retained between calls (as in C's strtok) that makes an API thread-unsafe, and prefer stateful-object interfaces such as StringTokenizer.

Always design for concurrency, because doing so up front keeps deployment flexible across standalone, client-server, or n-tier, and makes meeting scalability later easy, whereas retrofitting concurrency into a nonconcurrent application is much harder.
Separate a program into modules that each have a single, well-defined responsibility.
Use events (messages signaling that something interesting happened) to communicate state changes, which minimizes coupling because the sender needs no knowledge of the receivers.
Do not push all events through a single routine, because it violates encapsulation, increases coupling, and tends to violate DRY with a giant case or if-then.
Use a publish/subscribe protocol so objects register to receive only the events they need and are never sent events they do not (the Observer pattern).
Separate views from models: keep the data model separate from its views and from the controllers that manage those views (Model-View-Controller).

Loosening the coupling between model and view or controller buys large flexibility at low cost (multiple views of one model, common viewers across models, multiple controllers) and is a key way to maintain reversibility.

Apply Model-View-Controller as a general-purpose technique, not just for GUIs: the view interprets the model and need not be graphical, the controller coordinates, and the model has no knowledge of any view or controller.
Build model-viewer networks in which each link decouples raw data and each viewer is an abstraction, so one model can feed many viewers and one viewer can work with many models.
Use blackboards to coordinate workflow: a blackboard is a forum where producers and consumers exchange data anonymously and asynchronously, fully decoupling participants and reducing code.
A blackboard's participants need no knowledge of one another, can be heterogeneous, can come and go, and face no restriction on what they post.

Combine a blackboard with a rules engine to handle workflows with unpredictable data-arrival order, distributed asynchronous gathering, inter-data dependencies, and changing regulations, since posting a fact triggers the applicable rules and rule output can re-trigger more.
A single consistent blackboard interface avoids the combinatorial explosion of bespoke API calls that bogs down conventional distributed applications.
Partition and organize a cluttered blackboard, using flat interest zones or a hierarchical structure.

Treat coding as design work requiring thought and judgment, not mechanical transcription, because the attitude that coding is mechanical is a leading cause of ugly, unmaintainable, and wrong programs.
Recognize that developers who do not actively think about their code are programming by coincidence: the code may work, but for no particular reason.
Avoid programming by coincidence (relying on luck and accidental successes) and program deliberately instead, because if you do not know why code works you will not know why it fails.

Do not rely on a routine's undocumented error or boundary behavior, or call routines in an order or context they were not designed for, because when the routine is fixed your code breaks; rely only on documented behavior and document any assumption you must make.
Do not leave spurious calls in code just because it appears to work, since they may not truly work, may depend on accidents, may change with the next release, slow the code, and risk new bugs.
For code others will call, use good modularization, small well-documented interfaces, and an explicit contract to prevent misuse.
Do not depend on context that is not guaranteed, such as a GUI being present or users being English-speaking or literate.
Document your assumptions and test them with assertions rather than guessing, because undocumented and conflicting assumptions are the bane of projects.

Program deliberately: stay aware of what you are doing, do not build on technology you do not understand, proceed from a plan, rely only on reliable things and assume the worst when unsure, prioritize the hard fundamentals, and be willing to replace code that is no longer appropriate.
Estimate the time and memory an algorithm uses and especially how it scales with input size, because most significant algorithms are nonlinear and can degrade catastrophically as input grows.

Use big-O notation to bound how an algorithm's runtime or memory grows with input size, dropping low-order terms and constant factors, while remembering it hides constants so one O(n^2) algorithm can be far faster than another.

Estimate an algorithm's order from its structure: a simple loop is O(n), nested loops O(m x n), repeated halving O(lg n), divide-and-conquer O(n lg n), and permutation-based algorithms grow factorially.
Estimate the order of your algorithms: whenever you write loops or recursion, check how large the inputs can get and the effect on runtime and memory.
Address an O(n^2) algorithm by seeking a divide-and-conquer approach that brings it down to O(n lg n).
When unsure of an algorithm's runtime or memory, run it across varying input sizes and plot the results to reveal the shape of the curve.
Choose algorithms pragmatically: the asymptotically fastest is not always best, since a simple O(n^2) loop can beat a complex O(n lg n) one for small inputs and high setup or inner-loop costs.
Test your estimates, because the only timing that counts is your code running in production with real data; use profilers when accurate timing is hard.
Beware premature optimization: confirm that an algorithm really is a bottleneck before investing time improving it.
Treat software as gardening rather than construction, because code evolves organically and must be continually reworked rather than built once and left.
Refactor when you find duplication, nonorthogonal design, outdated knowledge or drifted requirements, or a need to improve performance.
Do not let time pressure be an excuse to skip refactoring, because fixing the problem later costs far more once more dependencies have accumulated.
Refactor early and refactor often: track what needs refactoring, schedule anything you cannot fix immediately, and tell affected users how it may impact them.
Refactor safely by not adding functionality at the same time, having good tests in place before you start and running them often, and taking short, deliberate steps with a test after each.
Make a drastically changed module's interface break the build so old clients fail to compile, letting you find and update every dependent quickly.
Treat the component-as-chip (Software IC) idea as valid only when components are known to be reliable, which requires designing them to be tested in the field, not just at build time.
Build testability into software from the beginning and test each piece thoroughly before wiring the pieces together.
Treat a unit test as code that exercises a module in isolation under controlled conditions, checking results against known values or prior runs (regression testing).

Test against contract: write tests that verify a unit honors its contract over a wide range of inputs and boundary conditions, which reveals both whether the code meets the contract and whether the contract means what you think.

Test a module's subcomponents first and then the module that depends on them, because if the subcomponent tests pass but the module's test fails, the fault is in the module or its use of them, which sharply narrows debugging.

Design to test: design a module's contract and the code that tests it together, and write the tests before implementing so you try the interface before committing and surface boundary conditions early.

Keep unit tests conveniently located (embedded for small projects, a subdirectory for large ones), because tests that are hard to find go unused, and accessible test code also documents how to use the module.
Ship the tests with the code so you can diagnose problems in the field.
Running tests is not optional: you must run them, and run them often.

Build a standard, composable test harness for the project with standard setup and cleanup, test selection, output analysis, and standardized failure reporting, and reuse an existing framework such as xUnit rather than writing your own.
Formalize ad hoc tests: when debugging produces a throwaway test, add it to the unit tests, because code that broke once is likely to break again.
Build a test window into deployed software (consistent-format log files, a hot-key diagnostic window, or a built-in web server for server code) to view internal state without a debugger.

Test your software, or your users will: all software gets tested eventually, so plan to test it thoroughly and instill a testing culture, which is more cultural than technical and works in any language.
Don't use wizard-generated code you don't understand, because it becomes interwoven with your own code and you will be unable to maintain or debug what you cannot explain.
Don't gather requirements, dig for them, because real requirements lie buried beneath assumptions, misconceptions, and politics rather than on the surface.

Separate requirements from policy: state the requirement as a general need and document changeable business policy separately and linked, so the design becomes a metadata-driven access-control system rather than hardwired tests.

Discover the underlying reason a user does something, not just how they currently do it, because your job is to solve their business problem rather than merely meet their stated requirements, and document those reasons for the team.
Work with a user to think like a user: spend time doing their job, such as sitting with the help desk, to gain real insight into how the system will be used and to build trust.

Capture requirements as abstract use cases rather than in user-interface terms, using a formal template as a checklist for performance, parties, priority, frequency, and errors, and allowing hierarchical nesting and cross-links.
Do not be a slave to any notation; use whatever method best communicates requirements to your audience, recognizing that true use cases are textual rather than stick-figure diagrams.

Do not overspecify requirements: keep the document abstract with the simplest statement that accurately reflects the business need, capturing semantic invariants as requirements and current practices as policy, because requirements are need, not architecture, design, or UI.

Abstractions live longer than details: invest in abstractions such as a DATE abstraction rather than embedding details, since failing to do so combined with violating DRY is what caused the Year 2000 problem.
Build tools that adapt to the hands that use them, leveraging users' existing skills and offering a comfortable transition through familiar metaphors to win buy-in.
Manage requirements creep by tracking requirements actively and showing project sponsors each new feature's impact on the schedule.

Use a project glossary: maintain one place defining every project-specific term and have all participants use it, since projects fail when people use different names for the same thing or the same name for different things.
Publish requirements and project documents as hypertext on internal web sites, so a diverse audience can drill to the level of detail each needs and the documents stay current.
Solve hard problems by identifying the real (not imagined) constraints and the degrees of freedom you actually have, honoring absolute constraints but challenging preconceived ones.
Don't think outside the box, find the box: when stuck, enumerate every possible avenue without dismissing any, then prove why each cannot work, and prioritize the most restrictive constraints first.

When a problem seems much harder than it should, step back and ask whether there is an easier way, whether you are solving the right problem, whether it must be done this way, and whether it must be done at all, because reinterpreting the requirements can dissolve the problem.
Listen to nagging doubts and start when you are ready, heeding instinct built from experience before beginning a task.

To tell good judgment from procrastination, prototype a difficult area as a proof of concept: boredom signals you were merely procrastinating, while a revelation that a premise was wrong shows your instinct was right.

Recognize that specification has diminishing or negative returns past a point, since no spec captures every nuance, natural language is inadequate, and an over-prescriptive design strips coding of skill and hides opportunities found only while coding.
Accept that some things are better done than described.

Treat requirements, design, and implementation as facets of one process of delivering a quality system, distrust isolated phases, and let feedback from implementation and testing flow back into the specification.

Reserve highly detailed specifications for life-critical systems and for interfaces or libraries used by others, and avoid layering specifications on specifications without supporting implementation or prototyping.
condition: detailed specifications are warranted for life-critical systems and for shared interfaces and libraries

statement: Don't be a slave to formal methods: never adopt a technique without fitting it to your team's practices and capabilities, and prefer letting users play with a prototype over diagrams they cannot actually check.

Never underestimate the cost of adopting new tools and methods, because their benefits appear only after a productivity and quality drop during adoption, so treat the first projects as a learning experience.

Use formal methods as one tool among many: extract the best from each, meld them into working practices, and continually refine your process rather than accepting a methodology's confines as the limits of your world.
Expensive tools do not produce better designs, so do not be swayed by a tool's cost or the false authority of a method, since the output is still a fallible interpretation of requirements.
Apply pragmatic techniques at the team level, not just the individual level, because their advantages multiply on a pragmatic team.
Treat quality as a team issue: the team as a whole should refuse to tolerate broken windows, because quality comes from every member's contributions, not from a delegated quality officer.

Guard teams against being slowly boiled: have everyone actively monitor for creeping scope, shrinking timescales, added features, and new environments, and stay aware of changes even when you do not reject them.
Have the team communicate to the outside world as one entity with structured meetings, consistent documentation, and a single voice, and give it an identity such as a project brand.
Appoint a project librarian to coordinate documentation and code repositories and spot impending duplication, and for larger projects appoint focal points for each functional area.

Organize around functionality, not job functions: split work into small, cohesive, largely self-contained teams that each own a functional aspect of the system, using the same modularization criteria you apply to code.
Do not silo analysis, design, coding, and testing into isolated groups, because they are different views of one problem and developers kept far from users cannot make informed decisions.

Organize teams with contracts, decoupling, and orthogonality so the team is isolated from change (a database-vendor switch should hit only the database team), which reduces cross-team interactions, shortens schedules, cuts defects, and increases ownership.

Functional team organization works only with responsible developers and strong management: a project needs both a technical head setting philosophy, assigning responsibilities, and watching overall orthogonality, and an administrative head scheduling, tracking progress, setting priorities, and liaising externally.
condition: requires responsible developers and strong project management

statement: Automate everything the team does to ensure consistency and accuracy, and appoint tool builders to construct the automation such as makefiles, scripts, and templates.
Give each team member room to shine and provide just enough structure to deliver against requirements, then resist the temptation to add more.

Don't use manual procedures: people are not as repeatable as computers, so use shell scripts and batch files kept under source control, and scheduled jobs such as cron, for consistent and repeatable operations.
Recognize that manual procedures leave consistency to chance, since multi-page manual setups produce subtly different environments and machine-specific bugs.

Build the project with makefiles even when using an IDE, because a scripted build is automatic and repeatable and can hook in code generation and regression tests, with the goal of checking out, building, testing, and shipping in a single command.
Use the build tool's dependency analysis to auto-generate files such as code, headers, and documentation from other sources.
Be wary of recursive make: it sees only the dependencies within a single invocation, so you can miss a needed rebuild or do extra work, and build dependencies may differ from test dependencies.

Treat a build as a procedure that, from an empty directory and a known environment, checks out the source, builds from a top-level makefile marked with a version, creates the distributable image, and runs the tests.

Run a full nightly build that executes all available tests, so a regression failure is caught close to the change that caused it; skipping regular testing means discovering breakage introduced months ago.
Use a separate target for final ship builds (locked or tagged repository, different optimization and debug flags), and retest whenever the product is compiled differently from earlier versions.

Generate and publish project web-site content automatically from the repository (build results, test results, metrics) as just another DRY view, because stale or misleading information is worse than none.
Automate administrative workflows such as code-review scheduling and approval, for example with status markers in source and web forms, to reduce the paperwork burden.
Let the computer do the repetitious, mundane work because it does a better job, and build your own tools with cron, make, and scripting languages rather than going without.
Test early, test often, and test automatically, because automated tests that run with every build beat shelved test plans and the earlier a bug is found the cheaper it is to fix.
Write test code at the same time as or before the production code, accept that a good project may have more test code than production code, and treat that effort as worthwhile for near-zero defects.
Coding is not done until all the tests run: you cannot claim code is usable by anyone until it passes every available test.
Perform the major testing types (unit, integration, validation and verification, resource exhaustion and recovery, performance, and usability) rather than relying on one.
Treat unit testing as the foundation and require every module to pass its own unit tests before proceeding, since parts that do not work alone will not work together.
Use integration testing to check that subsystems honor their contracts, because integration is often the single largest source of bugs and good contracts make integration issues easy to detect.

Validate and verify that the system meets the user's actual need, not merely what they said, because a bug-free system that answers the wrong question is useless; account for how end-user access patterns differ from developer test data.
Test behavior under real-world conditions, including resource exhaustion of memory, disk, CPU, and bandwidth, and graceful failure that saves state rather than crashing in the user's face.
Run performance, stress, and load testing to confirm the software meets its performance and scalability requirements under realistic load, using simulation tooling when needed.
Conduct usability testing with real users under real conditions, evaluated in terms of human factors.
Treat documentation as an integral part of development and as two views of one model, applying pragmatic principles such as DRY, orthogonality, and automation to it.
Treat English as just another programming language, and recognize that all documentation is a mirror of the code so that when they disagree the code is authoritative.
Build documentation in, don't bolt it on.

Comment on why something is done (its purpose, trade-offs, and discarded alternatives) not how, because the code already shows how and restating it violates DRY, while too many comments are as bad as too few.

Choose meaningful names and avoid meaningless ones such as foo and especially misleading ones such as a getData that writes, because misleading names cause real cognitive interference and code is read far more often than it is written.

Keep out of comments anything tools maintain better (exported-function lists, revision history, file lists, the filename), include the source file's author or owner to attach responsibility, and rely on source-control tags for the rest.
Use executable documents: pick one authoritative source for any repeated information and generate the other views (schema, code, documentation) from it automatically so they cannot disagree.

Involve technical writers as partners who follow the same principles (DRY, orthogonality, model-view, automation) rather than throwing material over the wall, and keep a document's presentation independent of its content by using markup such as XSL/CSS or DocBook to generate many formats from one source-controlled source published online with version stamps.
Perform usability testing as early as possible, while there is still time to correct, and treat a failure to meet usability criteria as just as serious a bug as dividing by zero.

Test the design and methodology by analyzing code metrics such as cyclomatic complexity, inheritance fan-in and fan-out, response set, and coupling ratios, using them comparatively across modules to flag outliers that may indicate problems.
Use regression tests that compare current output to previous or known values so that today's fixes do not break yesterday's working code, and run every kind of test as a regression.
Use both real-world and synthetic test data, because their different natures expose different bugs, with synthetic data covering volume, boundary conditions, and specific statistical properties.
Decouple application logic from the GUI so the logic can be tested without a user interface present, which also makes the remaining UI bugs easier to locate.

Use saboteurs to test your testing: after writing a test for a bug, deliberately cause that bug to confirm the test catches it, and optionally appoint a project saboteur to introduce bugs in a copy and verify the tests catch them.
Recognize you can never prove testing is thorough enough: coverage tools track executed lines but do not expect 100 percent, and executing a line is not the same as covering a state.
Test state coverage, not code coverage, because what matters is the number of program states, and the data used and the order in which code is traversed have the largest impact.

Start testing as soon as any production code exists rather than at the deadline, run most tests automatically including interpreting results automatically and always before checking code in, and put infrequent tests like stress tests on a regular scheduled basis.
Find bugs once: once a bug is found, modify the automated tests so that a human never has to find that same bug again.

Measure project success by how well it meets users' expectations, not just by correctly implementing the specification, because a project that falls below expectations is a failure regardless of its absolute quality.
Gently exceed your users' expectations, giving a little more than they expected without going so far that you disappoint them.

Communicate expectations throughout development so users' understanding of what you will deliver stays accurate, using tracer bullets and prototypes to show them something concrete and build a common understanding.

Go the extra mile to delight users with low-cost additions such as tooltips, keyboard shortcuts, a quick-reference guide, automated installation, and integrity tools, which pay off in goodwill without causing feature bloat or breaking the system.

Sign your work: take pride and responsibility in what you build, because anonymity breeds sloppiness, and ensure code is owned individually or communally with supporting practices such as pair programming.
A class that concentrates only on its own task and ignores incidental details such as where its input comes from is more orthogonal, making it both easier to develop and more flexible to reuse.

Object technology can yield a more orthogonal system than procedural code but is easier to abuse into a nonorthogonal one, because features like multiple inheritance, exceptions, operator overloading, and method overriding can increase coupling in nonobvious ways.
Modeless designs tend to be more orthogonal than modal ones, because modal designs build in assumptions about system state that increase coupling.
Keep contracts abstract: a postcondition that assumes a particular implementation, such as referencing internal indices or structure, is a bad contract.

Choose an error-handling strategy by how exceptional the condition is: raise an exception for out-of-memory, return an error for a normal lookup miss, and reserve an exception for a null argument only when null is meaningless to the application.
condition: null argument warrants an exception only when null values are meaningless to the application

statement: Never use gets(), because it writes as many characters as it receives into the buffer and has caused buffer-overrun security holes in many systems.
Do not bury user interaction in a library routine and do not assume a tty environment, that stderr and stdin are open, or that the user reads English.
Recognize that POSIX strcpy is not guaranteed to work for overlapping strings, so code that relies on it working is programming by coincidence.

When code may run in different contexts such as GUI versus non-GUI or an applet with security restrictions, check the environment dynamically rather than assuming capabilities such as writing a log file to the local disk.

In C and C++, set a pointer to NULL immediately after freeing the memory it references, because later dereferencing a NULL pointer usually raises a runtime error and catches rogue references to freed memory.
In long-running programs, set object references to null when finished so the object becomes eligible for garbage collection and memory use does not grow over time.

Have a header file declare only its interface, for example a forward class declaration, rather than include another class's full header, because pervasive includes drag in most of the system and slow compilation.

Under the Law of Demeter, call methods only on objects you own, were passed, or created, and ask the owning object for what you need rather than reaching into its subobjects, so its structural knowledge does not leak through its contract.

Replace a report that polls or trolls all records with a listener or observer design so entities report events themselves, for example a flight reporting when it is full, giving live updates instead of long batch runs.
Refactor enumerated type-codes that distinguish variants of a type into subclasses, replacing a switch-on-type with polymorphism.

Prefer delegation (has-a) over subclassing (is-a) when one class merely uses another's functionality, abstracting the varying part into its own type and defining an interface so the compiler flags affected classes.
Reduce recursion stack usage by allocating a single shared buffer passed as a parameter instead of a per-call local buffer, and by eliminating tail recursion and unnecessary leaf-node calls.

Represent volatile, frequently changing configuration such as port settings, editor syntax highlighting, or test data as metadata, while keeping performance-sensitive or device-driver concerns in code, optionally naming the driver in metadata and loading it dynamically.
Choose a blackboard over a simple shared work queue when feedback is involved, that is, when the result of processing one item affects the processing of others.

Build internal test drivers freely even when nothing in the requirements calls for them, such as driving a component via a small script language end users never see, because they let you test code quickly and exhaustively.
Make tests return process exit codes (zero for pass, nonzero for fail) so they compose into larger automated test runs.

Restate a requirement that fixes a specific appearance or value (such as dialog boxes being gray) as a configurability requirement (such as all visual elements being end-user configurable, gray as shipped), since the specific value is policy rather than requirement.

Translate a stated UI behavior into its underlying requirement (for example, beep on non-numeric input becomes prevent invalid entries and warn the user), capturing the need rather than the surface mechanism.
